summary: This standards track document describes Proportional Rate Reduction, an algorithm that regulates how much data TCP or similar protocols send during fast recovery. It obsoletes the experimental version in RFC 6937.

plainLanguage.summary: After a traffic jam, PRR lets cars back onto the road slowly, so the sender recovers smoothly.

questions: how does tcp fast recovery work
subtitle: A smoother way for TCP to cut its sending rate after packet loss, paced by the ACKs coming back.

tldr.problem: When TCP detects loss it has to shrink its window. Older fast recovery either goes quiet for part of a round trip or, after heavy loss, sends a large burst of data.
tldr.mechanism: PRR uses each ACK to work out how much data was delivered, then sends in proportion to that, so the amount in flight glides down to the target (ssthresh) and ends as close to it as possible.
tldr.outcome: This Standards Track version obsoletes the Experimental RFC 6937. It adds the SafeACK heuristic, defined behavior for connections without SACK, and setting cwnd to ssthresh at the end of recovery.

today: RFC 9937 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 6937, so it is the current specification of PRR. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Fast Recovery Needed Fixing
sections.content:
Congestion control algorithms such as Reno and CUBIC limit how much data is in flight with a congestion window (cwnd) and shrink it when packets are lost. Fast recovery is the step that makes this reduction using feedback from acknowledgments. Without PRR, fast recovery typically waits for a large fraction of a round-trip time before sending any data: one half round-trip time of ACKs for Reno or 30% of a round-trip time for CUBIC.

RFC 6675 improved on this by sending data on each ACK until its pipe estimate matches ssthresh. The RFC names two drawbacks. The large multiplicative decrease at the start can cause a timeout if the entire second half of the window of data or ACKs is lost. And one ACK with a SACK option implying lots of missing data can cause a step change in the estimator, so Fast Retransmit sends a large burst.

PRR is inspired by Van Jacobson's packet conservation principle: N segments delivered produce ACKs that clock out N more segments. Because it leans on that self clock, it is only slightly affected by errors in estimators such as the estimate of data in flight.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road gets jammed, old rules said either wait a long time or rush everyone out at once. PRR says: let one car out for each car that gets through.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 6937
sections.content:
The largest change is a new heuristic that picks between two Reduction Bounds. RFC 6937 left that choice to the implementer, recommending PRR-SSRB by default. Now the choice is made from recovery progress: a conservative default, with a switch to the faster bound only when ACKs show good progress.

The motivating case was traffic policing. Token bucket policers can suddenly start discarding a large fraction of traffic once tokens run out, with no warning to the end systems. There, PRR-CRB is too timid and PRR-SSRB too aggressive, and both lead to prolonged recovery. The SafeACK heuristic was experimented with in Google's CDN and implemented in Linux TCP since 2015.

  • RecoverFS now accounts for sequence ranges that were already SACKed before recovery began, so PRR no longer starts too slowly after reordering.
  • The first ACK that triggers recovery forces a fast retransmit, once per recovery, to keep the ACK clock going and avoid a retransmission timeout.
  • On exit from recovery the sender sets cwnd to ssthresh.
  • Behavior for connections that have not negotiated SACK is now specified.
  • PRR has also been adapted to window reductions for non-loss-based signals such as ECN.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules add a way to tell whether things are going well. If they are, PRR speeds up a little. If not, it stays careful.

sections.title: Where PRR Fits With Other Standards
sections.content:
PRR MAY be used with any congestion control algorithm that makes a multiplicative decrease over roughly one round-trip time, as long as in-flight data is limited by cwnd and the target during the reduction is a fixed value given by ssthresh. The RFC names Reno (RFC 5681) and CUBIC (RFC 9438). It is described as a modification to RFC 6675. It is most accurate with SACK but does not require it.

PRR has no dependency on how losses are detected. It only needs the loss detection algorithm to say how many packets were marked lost and how many were marked delivered. It MAY be used with Reno, NewReno, SACK, FACK and RACK-TLP. Because of RACK-TLP's resilience to tail loss, reordering and lost retransmissions, it is RECOMMENDED that PRR is implemented together with RACK-TLP (RFC 8985).
sections.plainLanguage: PRR is an add-on that works with many different ways of deciding how much to slow down and how to notice lost packets. It does not care which one is used.

sections.title: The PRR Algorithm
sections.content:
A sender using PRR MUST initialize PRR state at the start of each congestion control response episode, such as the start of fast recovery. It sets prr_delivered and prr_out to 0 and computes RecoverFS, the bytes the sender estimates might be delivered during the episode. RecoverFS starts as SND.NXT - SND.UNA, drops bytes already SACKed, and adds bytes newly SACKed and newly cumulatively acknowledged. It stays constant during the episode.

On each ACK the sender first computes DeliveredData, its best estimate of the bytes newly delivered. With SACK this is the change in SND.UNA plus the signed change in SACKed data. Without SACK it is estimated as 1 SMSS per duplicate ACK, capped so a misbehaving receiver cannot inflate it past RecoverFS. Next it estimates inflight, and then SafeACK, which is true only when the ACK cumulatively acknowledged new data and does not indicate further losses.

The sender then computes SndCnt, the number of bytes to send in response to the ACK. While inflight is above ssthresh, it sends in proportion to delivered data and ssthresh relative to RecoverFS. Once inflight is at or below ssthresh, it uses the Conservative Reduction Bound (PRR-CRB), which sends no more than was delivered, and adds one SMSS (the Slow Start Reduction Bound, PRR-SSRB) only when SafeACK is true. If nothing would otherwise be sent on the first ACK, one SMSS is sent as a forced fast retransmit. Every transmission adds to prr_out. When the episode ends, cwnd = ssthresh.

Setting cwnd to ssthresh at the end can allow a burst of back-to-back segments, so the RFC RECOMMENDS pacing to reduce burstiness. Which data to send (new or retransmitted) is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: PRR keeps two tallies: how much the other side got, and how much was sent. It only sends more when the first tally is ahead, and a little extra when things look healthy.

sections.title: Properties of PRR
sections.content:
PRR tries to preserve the sender's ACK clocking through recovery, including burst losses, where RFC 6675 can send large unclocked bursts. Normally it spreads voluntary window reductions evenly over a full RTT, which acts as a kind of soft pacing. The RFC notes that the burstiness benefits have not been quantified.

With minimal losses PRR converges to exactly the target window chosen by the congestion control algorithm. Isolated losses during recovery cause later voluntary reductions to be skipped. If the application stalls, the missed chances to send are banked, and the sender can later send a partial window burst to catch up, exactly as happens for a partial-RTT stall outside recovery.

Because inflight mostly decides which formula is used, rather than directly deciding how much to send, PRR is less sensitive to errors in that estimate than RFC 6675. Under all conditions, PRR-CRB strictly bounds data sent to no more than data delivered. Appendix A calls this the Strong Packet Conservation Bound: it is the most aggressive rule that does not cause additional forced losses in some environments, and it keeps a standing bottleneck queue at constant length. Measurements cited in RFC 6675 show it performs worse than RFC 6675 alone, so PRR-SSRB allows one extra segment per ACK when recovery is going well, while still being less aggressive than RFC 6675 under burst loss.
sections.plainLanguage: PRR never sends more than has just got through when things are shaky, so it does not add to the jam. When things look fine, it lets one extra car through each time.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC compares PRR with RFC 6675 in two scenarios. Both use bulk transfer, Reno, and cwnd = inflight = 20 segments, so ssthresh is 10 at the start of recovery.

In the first, a single segment is lost. Both algorithms send the same total amount of data. RFC 6675 experiences a "half window of silence" while PRR spreads the voluntary window reduction across an entire RTT.

In the second, the first 15 packets are lost and only 5 ACKs return in the lossy round trip. Here RFC 6675 is more aggressive: once Fast Retransmit triggers it immediately retransmits enough to bring inflight up to cwnd. PRR uses PRR-CRB and sends only as data is reported delivered. Once the fast retransmits are delivered and advance SND.UNA, PRR switches to PRR-SSRB, adding exactly one segment per ACK until inflight reaches ssthresh. This is still less aggressive than the single burst of RFC 6675. For less severe loss, where total losses are smaller than the gap between FlightSize and ssthresh, the bounds are never needed.
sections.plainLanguage: If one car is stuck, both methods are fine, but PRR lets cars out evenly. If lots of cars are stuck, the old method rushes many out at once, while PRR goes step by step.

sections.title: Deployment and Fairness
sections.content:
PRR is incrementally deployable. It uses only existing acknowledgment and loss-detection mechanisms and needs changes only at the data sender, with nothing required of receivers, routers, switches or other network devices. The RFC says PRR has extensive deployment experience in multiple TCP implementations since the first widely deployed one in 2011, and that in Linux TCP it has been the fast recovery algorithm for its default and supported congestion control modules since then.

It is designed to preserve the fairness, queuing and loss properties of the congestion control algorithm it is paired with, because it operates only during a response episode and does not change how cwnd grows or shrinks outside one. Over short time scales it aims for lower packet loss than RFC 6675, since it bases transmission on delivered data rather than lost data. The RFC says the main algorithm can be adapted to any transport that can support RFC 6675.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the sender has to learn the new trick, so nobody else needs to change anything. It also plays fair with other traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that PRR does not change the risk profile for transport protocols. It adds one caution: implementers who change PRR from counting bytes to counting segments must be careful about ACK splitting attacks, where a receiver acknowledges partial segments to confuse the sender's congestion accounting.

The algorithm also includes a guard against misbehaving receivers when SACK is not in use: the estimate of delivered data is capped so extra duplicate ACKs cannot push it past RecoverFS.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky receiver could try to trick the sender into thinking more has arrived than really has. PRR puts a cap on how much it will believe.

data.title: Per-ACK steps

viz.caption: THE THREE SENDING MODES IN PRR

items.title: Proportional
items.text: While inflight is above ssthresh, send in proportion to delivered data and ssthresh.

items.title: PRR-CRB
items.text: Below ssthresh, the default: send no more than was delivered (strict packet conservation).

items.title: PRR-SSRB
items.text: Below ssthresh with SafeACK true: send one extra segment per ACK.
